chunks.heading: Maple House Charter, Article I — Overnight Guests
chunks.text:
Members may host overnight guests in their own private rooms. Any single
guest may stay no more than two consecutive nights within any seven-day
period, so that no guest gradually becomes an unofficial resident of the
house. Whenever a guest is in the shared common areas, the hosting member
must accompany them. Each member is fully responsible for the conduct of
their guests for the entire duration of the visit.

chunks.heading: Maple House Charter, Article II — Quiet Hours
chunks.text:
Quiet hours are observed every night, running from 11:00 PM until 7:00 AM
the following morning. During quiet hours, conversation in the common areas
must be kept low, and any music, television, or video games must be played
through headphones. A member who anticipates unavoidable late-night noise
is required to give the rest of the house advance notice so that everyone
can reliably sleep.

chunks.heading: Maple House Charter, Article III — Kitchen Cleanup
chunks.text:
The kitchen must be cleaned by whoever used it, immediately after that
person finishes cooking or eating. Cleaning means washing every dish you
used, wiping down the counters and the stovetop, and taking out the trash
when the bin is full. Leaving dirty dishes in the sink overnight is never
permitted, no matter how late the hour or how tired the cook.

chunks.heading: Maple House Charter, Article IV — Common Spaces
chunks.text:
The living room, the dining room, and the back porch are common areas that
belong equally to every member of the house. No member may reserve a common
area for their own exclusive use, even temporarily, and no member may treat
a common area as a personal extension of their bedroom. These shared spaces
must remain open and available to all members at all times.

chunks.heading: Maple House Charter, Article V — Shared Chores
chunks.text:
All members share the household chores equally, following the rotating
weekly schedule posted in the kitchen. Every member is assigned the same
number of chore slots each month, and no member is exempt from the rotation
for any reason whatsoever. A member who cannot complete an assigned chore is
required to arrange a direct swap with another member ahead of time.

chunks.heading: Maple House Charter, Article VI — Pets
chunks.text:
No member may keep a pet of any kind in the house, with the single exception
of fish kept in a tank no larger than twenty gallons. This rule exists to
protect members who have allergies and to avoid noise, odor, and damage to
the shared furnishings. A member who wishes to pet-sit an animal for someone
outside the house must obtain unanimous consent from all members first.

chunks.heading: Maple House Charter, Article VII — Smoking
chunks.text:
Smoking of any kind is forbidden everywhere inside the house, including
inside a member's own private bedroom. The prohibition covers cigarettes,
cigars, pipes, and vaporizers alike. It exists to keep the shared air clean
and to reduce the risk of fire. Each member is responsible for ensuring that
their visitors also refrain from smoking indoors during any visit.

chunks.heading: Maple House Charter, Article VIII — Rent and Dues
chunks.text:
Each member must pay their share of the rent on or before the first day of
every month by transferring it to the house account. The monthly house dues
that cover shared cleaning supplies and paper goods are due on that same day.
A member who anticipates any difficulty paying on time is required to notify
the house treasurer before the first of the month.

chunks.heading: Maple House Charter, Article IX — Personal Belongings
chunks.text:
Members must keep their personal belongings in their own bedrooms or in
their assigned storage space. A personal item left in a common area for more
than one full day may be moved by any other member to the owner's bedroom
door. Perishable personal food left out in a common area may be thrown away
after a day. This keeps the shared spaces usable for everyone.

chunks.heading: Maple House Charter, Article X — House Decisions
chunks.text:
The house meets on the first Sunday of every month to make decisions
together. A decision passes by a simple majority of the members present, and
a recorded decision amends or extends this Charter from the date it is made.
Any member may place an item on the meeting agenda by posting it on the
kitchen board at least two days before the meeting.

chunks.heading: Decision — 2026-01-12 — Guest Logbook
chunks.text:
To keep track of who is in the house at any time, the members resolved that
every overnight guest must be signed into the guest logbook kept by the
front door, recording the guest's name and the dates of their stay. The
hosting member is responsible for making the entry before the guest's first
night. This record is meant to help with safety and accountability.

chunks.heading: Decision — 2026-02-10 — Weeknight Quiet Hours
chunks.text:
After repeated complaints about noise on work nights, the house met and
resolved to move the start of quiet hours earlier during the week. Effective
immediately, quiet hours now begin at 10:00 PM on Sunday through Thursday
nights, a full hour earlier than the Charter originally set. The 7:00 AM end
time and the Friday and Saturday start times are left unchanged.

chunks.heading: Decision — 2026-02-24 — Backyard Quiet
chunks.text:
Following complaints about late gatherings outdoors, the house resolved that
the quiet-hours rule also applies to the backyard and the back porch, not
only to the indoor common areas. During quiet hours, members and any guests
must keep outdoor conversation low and must not run outdoor speakers. This
decision extends the existing quiet hours rather than changing their times.

chunks.heading: Decision — 2026-03-14 — Guest Policy Revisited
chunks.text:
Following a long discussion about privacy, crowding, and the shared cost of
utilities, the house resolved to stop allowing overnight guests altogether.
Effective this month, overnight guests are no longer permitted in the house
at any time, for any number of nights, in any bedroom. Members may still
host visitors during the daytime, but every visitor must leave by 10:00 PM.

chunks.heading: Decision — 2026-03-28 — Guest Parking
chunks.text:
To settle ongoing confusion about where visitors should leave their cars,
the house resolved to set aside the two marked spaces at the far end of the
driveway specifically for visitor and guest parking. Guests are welcome to
leave a vehicle parked in those two spaces overnight without needing any
permit. This decision is strictly about parking and changes nothing about
whether or how long guests may stay in the house.

chunks.heading: Decision — 2026-04-02 — Cooking and Cleanup
chunks.text:
Recognizing that whichever member cooks dinner for the whole house already
contributes a great deal of effort, the house resolved that whoever cooks
the shared house dinner is excused from cleaning the kitchen on that night.
On those evenings, the work of washing the dishes, wiping the counters, and
taking out the trash falls instead to the members who sat down and ate.

chunks.heading: Decision — 2026-04-18 — Fridge Labeling
chunks.text:
To cut down on food going to waste and on disputes over groceries, the house
resolved that members must label their personal food in the shared
refrigerator with their name and the date it was placed there. Any unlabeled
food in the fridge may be treated as communal and eaten by anyone in the
house. This decision adds to the kitchen rules rather than replacing them.

chunks.heading: Decision — 2026-05-06 — Dining Room Reservations
chunks.text:
To make room for the occasional birthday or study group, the house resolved
that a member may reserve the dining room for their own private event up to
twice a month by signing the shared calendar at least three days ahead. For
the booked hours of a reserved event, the dining room is closed to the other
members so that the host can use the space.

chunks.heading: Decision — 2026-05-20 — Travel Chore Exemption
chunks.text:
Recognizing that several members travel frequently for work, the house
resolved that any member who is away from the house for more than two
consecutive weeks is fully exempt from the chore rotation for the entire
period they are gone. The remaining members will quietly cover the absent
member's chore slots, and the absent member owes no make-up chores on return.

chunks.heading: Decision — 2026-06-03 — House Cat
chunks.text:
After a heartfelt request and a long debate, the house resolved by majority
vote to allow one house cat, to be adopted and cared for collectively by the
members. The cat is permitted only if every current member gives written
approval beforehand, and it must be kept out of the bedroom of any member who
objects on the grounds of allergies.

chunks.heading: Decision — 2026-06-10 — Porch Smoking
chunks.text:
In response to requests from members who smoke, the house resolved that
smoking is now permitted outdoors on the back porch only, provided that the
smoker uses the sand bucket and sits at least ten feet away from any open
window. Smoking of every kind remains completely forbidden everywhere inside
the house, exactly as before.

chunks.heading: Decision — 2026-06-15 — Late Rent Fee
chunks.text:
To encourage everyone to pay on time, the house resolved that a member whose
rent share has not arrived in the house account by the fifth day of the
month owes an additional late fee of twenty-five dollars on top of the rent.
The treasurer will send a reminder to all members two days before the
monthly deadline.

chunks.heading: Maple House Charter, Article XI — Quiet Study Hours
chunks.text:
The dining room is set aside as a silent study space every weeknight from
7:00 PM until 9:00 PM. During those hours the dining room is reserved for
quiet individual work and may not be used for meals, conversation, or
gatherings. Members who need to eat during that window should use the
kitchen or their own rooms so that the study hours stay undisturbed for
those who are working.

chunks.heading: Decision — 2026-06-22 — Thursday Movie Nights
chunks.text:
To give the house a shared social evening, the members resolved to hold a
movie night in the living room on Thursday evenings. On those nights the
film and the conversation around it may run in the living room until
midnight, and any member who wishes to take part is welcome to stay up that
late. Members who would rather have quiet on a Thursday should plan around
the movie night.

tensions.reason: A guest staying in the hosting member's private room is not technically in a 'shared common area,' yet if that room has an open door or the host leaves to use the bathroom while the guest remains inside, it becomes impossible for the host to be present whenever the guest is in any shared space without violating the privacy implied by the first rule.

If a single guest stays for two consecutive nights and then returns on day four (within seven days), they are still within the limit of Rule 2; however, if their behavior causes significant disruption requiring intervention during this fragmented stay, the host must remain 'fully accountable' across non-consecutive periods where the guest has left and returned, creating an administrative burden that conflicts with the casual nature of short-term visits permitted by Rule 1.

Members are fully accountable for the behavior of their guests throughout the entire visit, yet members can only ensure visitors do not smoke indoors; they cannot physically prevent a determined adult from smoking inside a closed bedroom door against explicit instruction. A host who has done everything possible to enforce no-smoking rules is still held 'fully accountable' under the first commitment if a guest secretly smokes in their own room or another member's room while unobserved.

Quiet hours are strictly defined as running from 11:00 PM to 7:00 AM (Commitment 5), yet members may provide advance notice for 'unavoidable late-night noise' (Commitment 8). If a member gives notice and then makes noise at midnight, they have technically violated the quiet hour rule unless the notice itself constitutes an exemption. The Charter does not state that notice *waives* the quiet hours, only that it is provided. Thus, one cannot both fully honor the strict time-bound silence of Commitment 5 and allow the noisy activity implied by Commitment 8 without an explicit override mechanism.

Common areas must not be reserved for exclusive use (Commitment 12), but personal belongings are kept in assigned storage or bedrooms (Commitment 14). If a member's 'assigned storage space' is located within a common area (e.g., a specific shelf in the living room), keeping their items there effectively reserves that portion of the common area for their exclusive use, violating Commitment 12. The tension exists because Commitment 14 allows designated spaces which may physically reside in shared zones, conflicting with the non-exclusivity rule.

Personal items found in common areas after one day are moved to the owner’s door (Commitment 15), but perishable food left in common areas is discarded if left for a day (Commitment 16). If an item is both personal and perishable (e.g., a half-eaten sandwich on a plate), it falls under both rules. One cannot simultaneously move it to the owner's door (preserving it) and discard it (destroying it). The situation forces a choice between respecting property rights via relocation or enforcing hygiene/safety via disposal.

Items must be posted no less than two days prior to the meeting (Commitment 20), which occurs on the first Sunday of each month (Commitment 17). If the first Sunday is the 1st of the month, items must be posted by the previous month’s last day. However, if a member anticipates difficulty making payments, they must notify the treasurer by the end of the *previous* month (Commitment 13). While not directly conflicting with agenda posting, the tension arises if a financial issue needs to be discussed at the meeting: it requires both notification to the treasurer and an agenda item. The strict 'two days prior' rule for agendas might conflict with urgent financial disclosures that are only finalized in the final days before the deadline, though this is weak. A stronger tension is between Commitment 20 and Commitment 18/19 regarding emergency amendments? No. Let's look closer. Actually, there isn't a strong direct logical contradiction here unless we assume 'no less than two days' means exactly 48 hours vs calendar days. This pair is likely not a valid tension under precision rules.

The hosting member must be present whenever a guest is in common areas (Commitment 3), but music/games are played through headphones during quiet hours (Commitment 7). If the host is playing video games with their guest in the living room at midnight using headphones, they satisfy Commitment 7 regarding noise source control. However, if the game involves verbal communication or movement that generates ambient sound beyond just audio output, it may violate the spirit of 'low conversation' (Commitment 6) or general quietness. More directly: Commitment 3 requires presence, implying active supervision/interaction. If the interaction required for supervision necessitates speaking above a whisper to be heard over background house noises (even if low), it conflicts with keeping conversation low (Commitment 6). The situation is supervising a child guest during quiet hours where normal conversational volume exceeds the allowed limit.

Commitment 1 explicitly permits overnight guests to stay in a private room, while Commitment 15 states that overnight guests are not permitted in the house at all. A situation where a member wishes to host an overnight guest creates a direct conflict between allowing their presence and prohibiting it.

Commitment 2 allows a single guest to stay for up to two consecutive nights within a seven-day period, implying they may remain past midnight on those nights. However, Commitment 16 requires all visitors to leave by 10:00 PM, making it impossible for a guest to fulfill the 'consecutive night' requirement without violating the departure time rule.

On a Thursday evening when the dining room is reserved for an event (Commitment 13), it must remain closed to all other members. However, Commitment 24 permits activity in the living room until midnight during movie nights; if any participating member needs to use the kitchen or bathroom located near or through the dining area, they are blocked by the reservation rule while still being allowed to stay up late under the movie night exception.

Quiet hours begin at 11:00 PM every night (Commitment 5). On Thursday evenings, movie night participants are permitted to continue their activities in the living room until midnight (Commitment 24), creating a one-hour window where noise from the movie is explicitly allowed despite the general quiet hour mandate.

A member is physically unable to perform their assigned chore due to a sudden medical emergency or disability. Commitment 'No member is ever exempted from participating in the chore rotation under any circumstances' forbids exemption, while commitment 'Any member unable to perform their assigned chore must proactively arrange a direct exchange with another household member before the scheduled time' requires an action (arranging an exchange) that may be impossible if the inability arises suddenly without prior notice or capacity.

If fewer than half of the household members attend a meeting and vote against a proposal submitted by another minority group, the simple majority present can reject it even though more total members in the house might support it; however, if the quorum is too low for any decision to be valid (implied by standard governance logic often paired with such rules), or simply if the 'majority present' rule allows a small subset to override the will of absent majorities who had no chance to add items due to the two-day notice period.

Commitment 'Overnight guests are not permitted in the house' prohibits anyone from staying inside after dark, while commitment 'Visitors may park their vehicles in the designated spaces overnight without requiring a permit' explicitly allows visitors to remain on the property (in their cars) past midnight. A visitor who arrives late and chooses to sleep in their car rather than leave entirely creates a situation where they are simultaneously an 'overnight guest' present at the residence but excluded from the interior.

A member wishes to host a private dinner party for friends arriving unexpectedly or with short notice; however, commitment 'Reservations must be made by signing the shared calendar at least three hours in advance of the event' makes it impossible to honor the right to reserve the space ('reserve the dining room... no more than two times per month') if less than three hours have elapsed since the decision was made.

A member who is away from the house for more than two consecutive weeks must be fully exempted from the chore rotation during their absence, which directly contradicts the rule that no member is ever exempted under any circumstances.

The prohibition of pets in the house except for fish conflicts with the allowance to keep a house cat after obtaining written approval, as keeping a cat violates the explicit exclusion of all other animals.

The commitment that 'Overnight guests are not permitted in the house' directly contradicts the requirement that 'Every overnight guest is signed into the guest logbook,' as a situation involving an actual overnight guest cannot satisfy both prohibitions and procedural requirements simultaneously.

A hosting member attempting to fulfill the duty of making a 'guest logbook entry before the guest’s first night' for an overnight stay violates the rule that 'Overnight guests are not allowed in the house.'

On Thursday evenings between 7:00 PM and 9:00 PM, the dining room is designated as a silent study space where eating and talking are prohibited, while simultaneously movie nights occur in the living room; if participants wish to eat or socialize during this specific two-hour window before the movie fully takes over or as part of the evening's start, they cannot use the dining room due to its exclusive status as a quiet zone, forcing them to either wait until 9:00 PM or find another location not specified for such use.

A member reserves the dining room for a private event on a weeknight between 7:00 PM and 9:00 PM; while 'The dining room remains closed to all other members during the booked hours', it simultaneously must serve as a silent study space open to everyone.

During a reserved event in the dining room that overlaps with the 7:00-9:00 PM window on a weeknight, the room is occupied by the reserver but also required to remain quiet and unused for eating or social gatherings.
